extracted.intended_audience: educated public, political thinkers, and policymakers interested in constitutional government and the role of monarchy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and normative criteria about the institution and functions of a constitutional monarchy (its social role, ceremonial splendour, reserve powers, relationship to Cabinet government, and limits of active duties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court splendour vs. mean court
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are arguments for not having a Court, and there are arguments for having a splendid Court; but there are no arguments for having a mean Court. It is better to spend a million in dazzling when you wish to dazzle, than three-quarters of a million in trying to dazzle and yet not dazzling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court should either properly fulfil a role of splendour (when spectacle is intended) or not pretend to it; a half-hearted, 'mean' court that attempts to dazzle but fails is worse than no court at all. Comparison with continental (e.g., French) models must account for different constitutional ideas (Emperor vs. Queen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy as a 'disguise' enabling peaceful change
rubrics_metrics.description: “It acts as a DISGUISE. It enables our real rulers to change without heedless people knowing it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the greatest utilities of constitutional royalty is to obscure the mechanics of governmental change from a public unfit for direct elective government; this concealment helps preserve order and smooth transitions without alarming or destabilising popular sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the mystery/secret prerogative of the Crown
rubrics_metrics.description: “Its mystery is its life. We must not let in daylight upon magic. We must not bring the Queen into the combat of politics, or she will cease to be reverenced by all combatants; she will become one combatant among many.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public investigations or select committees into the sovereign risk destroying the reverence and utility of the Crown; some degree of secrecy about royal prerogatives is considered essential to the effectiveness of constitutional royalty in the author's view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid burdening the sovereign with trivial/formal routine duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Queen has to assent to and sign countless formal documents ... commissions in the army ... Till an Act passed only three years since the Queen used to sign ALL military commissions, and she still signs all fresh commissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine administrative signings are trivial, cause backlog or absurd delays (commissions received years late), and are not the source of royal authority; such formal labours should be dismissed or delegated so the sovereign is not consumed by slavish routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect the sovereign to guarantee domestic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: “We have come to regard the Crown as the head of our morality... But a little experience and less thought show that royalty cannot take credit for domestic excellence... It is not rational to expect the best virtue where temptation is applied in the most trying form at the frailest time of human life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although monarchy is popularly seen as a moral exemplar, the author cautions against relying on constitutional monarchs to provide domestic virtue: the temptations and unique circumstances of princes often make such expectations unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarch as reserve power useful in times of transition
rubrics_metrics.description: “The traditional strength of the hereditary monarch is at these times of incalculable use... It would have been impossible for England to get through the first years after 1688 but for the singular ability of William III. It would have been impossible for Italy to have attained and kept her freedom without the help of Victor Emmanuel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitutional monarch can provide invaluable stabilising authority and support to new Cabinet governments or in national transitions, strengthening insecure premiers and facilitating the establishment of new forms of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarch may (if wise and disinterested) select a superior Premier when parties are divided
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the constitutional monarch be a man of singular discernment, of unprejudiced disposition, and great political knowledge, he may pick out from the ranks of the divided party its very best leader, even at a time when the party, if left to itself, would not nominate him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the dominant party is internally divided, a discerning, impartial sovereign can identify and appoint a statesman who would best unify and lead; this is a conditional advantage of royal appointment over a pure parliamentary selection in such circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of prejudice in sovereign's judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is great danger, too, that the judgment of the sovereign may be prejudiced... For more than forty years the personal antipathies of George III. materially impaired successive administrations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The benefit of royal selection depends on the sovereign's qualities; ordinary, prejudiced, or narrowly experienced monarchs can do more harm than good by preferring mediocre or personally liked candidates over truly able leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating the head of society with the head of State
rubrics_metrics.description: “Society as such has no more to do with civil polity than with ecclesiastical. The organisation of men and women for the purpose of amusement is not necessarily identical with their organisation for political purposes... There is no naturalness in uniting the two; the end of it always is, that you put a man at the head of society who very likely is remarkable for social defects, and is not eminent for social merits.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The social leadership of 'society' (pleasure, conversation, fashion) should not be identified with political leadership; mixing these roles tends to elevate people chosen for social qualities rather than for governance ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make highest social rank an open elective prize
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the highest post in conspicuous life were thrown open to public competition, this low sort of ambition and envy would be fearfully increased... Politics would offer a prize too dazzling for mankind; clever base people would strive for it, and stupid base people would envy it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening the most conspicuous social positions to popular competitive election risks encouraging vulgar ambition and envy, increasing the number of social adventurers and degrading public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise that many royal prerogatives are in a twilight state and need clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: “If any one will run over the pages of Comyn's Digest or any other such book, title 'Prerogative,' he will find the Queen has a hundred such powers which waver between reality and desuetude, and which would cause a protracted and very interesting legal argument if she tried to exercise them. Some good lawyer ought to write a careful book to say which of these powers are really usable, and which are obsolete.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is uncertainty about which ancient royal powers remain usable; the author recommends clarifying by legal scholarship which prerogatives are operative and which are effectively obsolete to remove ambiguities in a popular government.

rubrics_metrics.name: The sovereign's effective executive role is limited in modern constitutional practice
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the bare superficial theory of free institutions this is undoubtedly a defect. Every power in a popular Government ought to be known... That secrecy is, however, essential to the utility of English royalty as it now is.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While older theory may imagine the sovereign as a co-ordinate estate or as the executive, modern practice places real executive power with the Prime Minister and Cabinet; the sovereign's active legislative veto is effectively gone, and much of the sovereign's authority is ceremonial or discretionary in secret.
